summary: Specifies how to set up and maintain pseudowires with the Label Distribution Protocol, emulating Layer 2 services such as Ethernet over an MPLS network. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire carries a Layer 2 service across an MPLS network. RFC 8077 defines how the edge routers use LDP to set up the pseudowire, identify it with a label, and report its status.

questions: how does ldp set up a pseudowire
what is the pwid fec element
what is the control word in a pseudowire
subtitle: Uses LDP to establish and maintain point-to-point pseudowires over an MPLS-enabled network.

tldr.problem: Layer 2 services can be carried over an MPLS network using pseudowires, but the two edge routers need to agree on which label identifies each pseudowire and how to report its status.
tldr.mechanism: The routers use LDP label mappings with a pseudowire Forwarding Equivalence Class identifier. Status TLVs report faults, and a control-word bit signals whether that field is used.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8077 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 4447 and RFC 6723. It adds procedures for renegotiating control-word use.

today: RFC 8077 is Internet Standard STD 84, published in February 2017. It obsoletes RFC 4447 and RFC 6723.

sections.title: The Pseudowire and Its Endpoints
sections.content:
A pseudowire emulates a Layer 2 service, such as Ethernet, Frame Relay, or ATM, over a packet-switched network. Other documents define how the Layer 2 frames are encapsulated; RFC 8077 defines how the endpoints establish and maintain the pseudowire using extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

The specification covers point-to-point pseudowires. It assumes an MPLS-capable tunnel can carry the packets, but the procedures for setting up that tunnel are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire carries an emulated Layer 2 service between two endpoints. This RFC explains how those endpoints use LDP to set it up and maintain it.

sections.title: How the Pseudowire Label Is Used
sections.content:
The PW label identifies the pseudowire at the receiving edge router. Many pseudowires can share a packet-switched network tunnel, so the network core does not need to keep state for each pseudowire.

The sender places the PW label at the bottom of the MPLS label stack. If the tunnel uses an MPLS Label Switched Path, the sender pushes a tunnel label above it. Each direction is set up independently, and the two directions are bound into a bidirectional pseudowire.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving edge router uses the PW label to identify which pseudowire carried a packet. A tunnel label can carry that packet through the MPLS network.

sections.title: Two Ways to Identify a Pseudowire
sections.content:
An LDP Label Mapping message carries a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) that identifies the pseudowire associated with a label. The PWid FEC element, type 0x80, is used when both endpoints have been provisioned with the same 32-bit pseudowire identifier.

The Generalized PWid FEC element, type 0x81, identifies the two endpoints using an Attachment Group Identifier, a Source Attachment Individual Identifier, and a Target Attachment Individual Identifier. Only one of the two FEC elements is used for a given pseudowire.
sections.plainLanguage: One FEC type identifies a pseudowire with a shared number. The other identifies it using information about its endpoints.

sections.title: Establishing and Reporting Pseudowire Status
sections.content:
With the Generalized PWid FEC, one edge router sends a Label Mapping containing the endpoint identifiers. If the receiving router can map the target identifier to a forwarder, it accepts the mapping and ensures that a pseudowire LSP exists in the reverse direction. The two directions use reversed source and target identifiers.

The PW Status TLV reports one or more fault bits in an LDP Notification message. The endpoints negotiate whether to use that TLV during setup; if it is not supported by both, they use label withdrawal to signal status changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers exchange label mappings to establish both directions of the pseudowire. They can report faults with a status TLV or use label withdrawal when that method is not supported.

sections.title: Negotiating the Control Word
sections.content:
The optional control word sits between the MPLS label stack and the payload. The C-bit in the FEC indicates whether the control word is present. Some pseudowire types require it; other types let each endpoint prefer or not prefer its use.

For types where it is optional, the control word is used only if both endpoints prefer it. If an endpoint is reconfigured, it can restart negotiation with Label Withdraw, Label Release, and Label Request messages, then follow the normal C-bit procedure again.
sections.plainLanguage: The C-bit reports whether a pseudowire uses a control word. For types where it is optional, both endpoints must agree to use it.

sections.title: Data-Plane and Control-Plane Security
sections.content:
The pseudowire encapsulation does not by itself authenticate the sender, protect packet integrity, or provide privacy. The RFC says the MPLS network should be isolated from unauthorized packet insertion and should not accept external MPLS packets unless the top label was legitimately distributed.

For the control plane, an incoming LDP session must come from an eligible peer, and source-address spoofing must be prevented. Implementations must support the LDP MD5 authentication option; the RFC recommends using it for greater security, while noting that it does not provide privacy and offers limited replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The label exchange does not encrypt or authenticate the Layer 2 traffic itself. LDP control sessions should be limited to eligible peers and protected against spoofing.
